quote: Ob eine [-...-] etwa ternäre Form {+der+} geraden Ordnung und definit {+ist,+} sich als Summe von positiven Potenzen linearer Formen darstellen lässt, [-...-] ist wahr- scheinlich einfach daran geknüpft, ob die Kanonisante positiv aus- fällt.
english: Whether a, say, ternary form of even order that is definite can be represented as a sum of positive powers of linear forms is probably simply tied to whether the Kanonisante turns out positive.
topic: The page first finishes a calculus-of-variations remark about an endpoint constrained to a surface and the independence theorem. It then asks whether a definite ternary form of even order can be written as a sum of positive even powers of linear forms, linking this to the sign of the 'Kanonisante' and to the stability of such representations under small perturbations.

triage.modern_statement: Let f be a real form of even degree 2d in n variables (Hilbert takes n = 3) that is positive definite. When can f be written as f = Σ_k (α_k·x)^{2d}, a sum of 2d-th powers of real linear forms with positive coefficients? Equivalently, when does f lie in Reznick's cone Q_{n,2d}? Hilbert guesses that this is decided by one sign condition: that the 'Kanonisante' (most likely Sylvester's canonizant, i.e. the catalecticant/Hankel determinant or quadratic form of f) is positive. In modern terms, the question is whether membership in Q_{n,2d} is the same as positivity of the middle catalecticant.
triage.answered_by: This is now a well-developed theory, mainly due to Bruce Reznick, 'Sums of Even Powers of Real Linear Forms' (Memoirs AMS vol. 96, no. 463, 1992), with later quantitative work by G. Blekherman (Israel J. Math. 2006). It rests on the duality between the cone of sums of powers and the cone of nonnegative forms, and on Hilbert's own 1888 theorem. The standard theory gives a split answer: a catalecticant (Hankel) positivity condition does decide the question for binary forms and for ternary quartics. It does not decide it in general, for example ternary sextics, because there are nonnegative forms that are not sums of squares. Positive definiteness of f alone is also far from sufficient. My searches did not turn up a source that discusses Hilbert's diary remark directly.

evidence.claim: Reznick's 1992 AMS Memoir began a systematic study of writing real forms of even degree as sums of powers of linear forms.
Memoir details: Reznick, Sums of Even Powers of Real Linear Forms, Memoirs AMS vol. 96 (1992), 155 pp.
Reznick's slides use the cone Q_{n,m} of sums of m-th powers, show it lies inside the convex forms, and use the generalized Hankel matrix (catalecticant) as the tool for testing membership.

Blekherman compares nonnegative forms, sums of squares and sums of powers of linear forms. When the degree is above two, there are significantly more sums of squares than sums of powers of linear forms. So positive definiteness does not imply being a sum of even powers.
Hilbert (1888): every positive semidefinite ternary quartic is a sum of three squares of quadratic forms. By duality, this is why the catalecticant criterion works for ternary quartics.

Hilbert used linear relations to show that sums of squares form a proper subset of the nonnegative forms on the Veronese surface ν3(P2), i.e. ternary sextics. By duality, the catalecticant condition fails to characterize sums of sixth powers there.
Recent work on real ranks of ternary quartics still uses the signature of the middle catalecticant.

triage.why: The note is a real research question: which definite forms are positive sums of even powers of linear forms. It became the subject of Reznick's 1992 Memoir and later work by Blekherman and others on the cone Q_{n,2d}. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Hilbert's 'one sign condition' guess holds in the cases where nonnegative forms and sums of squares coincide: binary forms and ternary quartics, where a positive catalecticant is the right test. It fails for ternary forms of degree 6 and higher. That last step comes from my own duality argument (sums of powers are dual to nonnegative forms, sums of squares are dual to forms with positive semidefinite catalecticant) applied to Hilbert's 1888 results. None of the snippets I retrieved says it outright, and my last searches to confirm the binary and duality statements were cut off by the tool limit. Confidence is medium because 'Kanonisante' could mean something slightly different from the catalecticant. The area is still active: real rank, sums of powers and cone geometry are all current topics.
